The Short-clawed Lark (Certhilauda chuana) is a medium-sized passerine inhabiting the semi-arid savannas of southern Africa. Eggs placed in an incubated nest at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after a period of approximately 15 days [ab = approximately 15 days], though field records indicate this can range between 14 and 16 days depending on microclimatic conditions. The altricial nestlings emerge weighing only 3.98 grams [Wwb = 3.98 grams], a remarkably low neonatal mass for a bird of this body size, reflecting the substantial energetic investment required during the subsequent brooding period. Nestlings are brooded intensively by the female while the male provisions, a biparental strategy that accelerates early growth. The downy chicks develop rapidly under the constant care of both parents, transitioning from ectothermic reliance on brooding to independent thermoregulation as their feather tracts emerge.

As the nestling period progresses, feather growth accelerates and the young birds approach the critical milestone of fledging. Under the thermal conditions typical of the active breeding season, measured at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at fledging is recorded as 49 days since birth [tx = 49 days since birth], although some studies document a range of 6 to 8 weeks for this developmental transition. The fledglings, once they achieve their first flight, remain dependent on parental provisioning for several additional weeks while they hone their foraging skills on the open ground. This extended post-fledging care period is likely an adaptation to the unpredictable prey availability characteristic of the species' arid habitat, where grasshoppers and beetle larvae can be patchily distributed. The departure of the nestlings from the nest cup, however, marks a definitive shift toward independence.

Sexual maturation in Certhilauda chuana follows a predictable timeline, although notable intraspecific variation exists between populations. In the same thermal environment of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that characterizes the breeding season, the time since birth at puberty is estimated at 147 days [tp = 147 days], with some accounts suggesting a range of 6 to 8 weeks for the attainment of gonadal activity. This relatively rapid maturation compared to larger-bodied alaudids may reflect selective pressures for early breeding in an environment where suitable nesting windows are constrained by rainfall patterns. Juveniles that fledge early in the spring rains are more likely to reach reproductive maturity within their first year. The onset of gametogenesis is accompanied by pronounced changes in the song behavior of males, who establish territories through vocal displays.

The timing of the first reproductive event for this lark is closely tied to its life-history strategy in a stochastic environment. At the same elevated body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that supports peak metabolic activity, the time since birth at first brood is typically 365 days [tR = 365 days], meaning most individuals commence breeding at approximately twelve months of age. This annual cycle is synchronized with the summer rains that drive invertebrate abundance and thereby ensure adequate food for provisioning chicks. In the western population, females typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], laying an average of 2.75 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2.75 eggs per clutch]. The eastern population, by contrast, lays fewer eggs per clutch, averaging 2.27 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2.27 eggs per clutch], but compensates by initiating up to 5 clutches per year, enabling a higher total reproductive output. This flexibility in reproductive rate reflects a life-history strategy that balances the risks of nesting failure against the energetic demands of repeated egg production.

Longevity records for the Short-clawed Lark reveal a life-history trade-off common among arid-zone passerines. Under field conditions experienced at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years], a figure derived from mark-recapture studies of color-banded individuals. This relatively long lifespan for a lark of its size is likely an adaptation to the unpredictable nature of its environment, where years of drought may drastically reduce annual reproductive success. Females achieve an ultimate wet weight of 30.4 grams [Wwi = 30.4 grams], while males are consistently heavier, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 38.1 grams [Wwi = 38.1 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism may be linked to male-male competition for territories and the energetic demands of song display. Senescent individuals begin to show reduced feather quality and lower provisioning rates, typically succumbing to physiological death during the harsh dry season.
